title: Folio 2: Two Brothers, One Throne
description: In the spring of 1030, the great Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni dies, and his empire is left to the wrong son. His elder son Masud is far away in Isfahan, and his younger son Muhammad is already on the throne. Over six tense months, letters fly, armies change sides, and a kingmaker learns the price of making kings. Beyhaqi, who knew these men, tells us how it really went.
source: Tarikh-e Beyhaqi, the surviving part of volume five: the letter from Tiginabad, the arrest of Hajib Ali in Herat, and Masud's arrival in Balkh (421 AH / 1030 CE)
cold_open: A camp in the hills of southern Afghanistan, in the autumn of the year one thousand and thirty. A young king wakes up to find that his army belongs to someone else. By evening, he is a prisoner in a fortress. And a letter is already on its way to his brother.
paragraphs: Welcome to The Honest Historian. I'm Mehdi Rahmani, and this is Folio Two. Last week, we stood with the crowd in Balkh and watched a proud vizier die on the gallows. Today, I want to go back a little, to the months that made that day possible.
Because before Masud could punish anyone, he had to become Sultan. And in the year one thousand and thirty, that was not at all certain. He had a rival, and his rival was his own brother.

Let me introduce the family. Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni ruled a huge empire, from the edge of India in the east to the cities of central Iran in the west. His capital, Ghazni, sits in the mountains of what is now Afghanistan. Mahmud had two sons who matter for our story. Masud was the elder. Muhammad was the younger, and some sources say the two were born in the same year, perhaps even twins.

For a long time, Masud was the chosen heir. His father made him governor of Herat, the beautiful city in the west of today's Afghanistan, when he was still a young man. Masud led armies. He fought in the mountains of Ghur. He was bold, generous, quick to act, and very popular with the soldiers.

But father and son did not get along. Mahmud was a hard, suspicious ruler, and Masud was a prince who did not like to be told what to do. Near the end of his life, Mahmud changed his mind. He gave the western lands, the newly conquered city of Ray and the lands around it, to Masud. And he named Muhammad, the quieter son, with far less experience of war, as his heir to the throne in Ghazni.
In other words, he sent the strong son far away, and kept the weaker son close.
At the end of April, in the year one thousand and thirty, Sultan Mahmud died in Ghazni.

Masud was in Isfahan, in the middle of Iran, at that time. He was busy with his own plans. He had been thinking of marching further west, to Hamadan, and perhaps even to Baghdad, the seat of the caliph. Ghazni was nearly a thousand miles away.

Meanwhile, in the capital, the great men of the court made a quick decision. They followed the old Sultan's will. They brought Muhammad from Guzganan, the province he governed in the north, and placed him on the throne.

Three men stood behind him. The first was the commander of the army, a Turkish general named Ali Qarib, whom Beyhaqi usually calls Hajib Ali, which means Ali the Chamberlain. The second was Yusuf, the brothers' own uncle. And the third was a name you know from last week: the vizier Hasanak. So when Hasanak said, if Masud ever becomes king, let them hang me, he was not speaking in the abstract. He was standing on the other side.
For a few months, Muhammad was Sultan. But, as Beyhaqi lets us see, the real business of the state was in the hands of Hajib Ali.
Masud did not rush blindly toward Ghazni. He did something clever first. He wrote to his brother.

We know about this letter because Masud mentions it himself, later, in a private note to the generals. He says that he sent his brother a message of condolence for their father, and of congratulation, and of advice. And he claims that if Muhammad had accepted that advice, he would have shared power with him. Whether Masud really meant it, we cannot know. But it allowed him to say, afterwards, that he had offered peace first, and that his brother had refused it.

Then Masud began to move. He gave up the idea of Baghdad. He marched east, from Isfahan to Ray, then to Nishapur, the great city of Khorasan. There, it is said, an envoy of the caliph in Baghdad reached him with a document recognizing him as the ruler of his father's lands. That was powerful support. Soldiers and officials began to drift toward him, one by one. By the autumn, Masud was in Herat, his old city, close to the heart of the empire.
Now, at last, Muhammad marched out of Ghazni with his army to face his brother. He got as far as a place called Tiginabad, in the dry country of southern Afghanistan, near the old town of Bust.
And there, his army simply left him.

It was not a battle. No swords were drawn. Hajib Ali and the other commanders quietly sent word to Masud that they were now his men. Even the uncle, Yusuf, went over. On the third day of the month of Shawwal, in the Islamic year four hundred and twenty one, which fell in early October of one thousand and thirty, Muhammad was deposed. He was taken, with his family and his servants, to a fortress at Tiginabad called Kuhtiz, and placed under guard.
And here is where Beyhaqi becomes precious to us. Because he does not just tell us that this happened. He copies the actual letter that the generals sent to Masud that very day.

It is a remarkable document. The men who had put Muhammad on the throne five months earlier now explain, very politely, that God's decree always runs the way God wills. Muhammad's reign, they say, was only a temporary arrangement. The rightful king has now appeared. They had only been obeying the late Sultan's orders. And would His Majesty please forgive them, and tell them what to do with his brother.
If you have ever read a statement from a company that has just changed sides, you know this tone. It has not changed much in a thousand years.

Beyhaqi also gives us a glimpse of Muhammad himself, the young man left behind in the fortress. For two or three days, we are told, he was lost in sorrow and would not speak. A few days later, envoys came up to the fortress with a letter from Masud. Muhammad would stay in Kuhtiz, honorably, with his household, but under guard. When he read it, he grew visibly troubled.
And one of the envoys, a wise old official, told him to be patient and accept what God had decided. Then he said three short Persian words. Budani bude ast. What was meant to be, has been.
It is a gentle sentence. It is also a door closing.

Now, what about the kingmaker, Hajib Ali? He had made one Sultan and then unmade him. He must have felt very safe. Masud had written to him with warm praise and told him to come to Herat with the army, the elephants and the treasury, and promised that the affairs of the state would be in his hands.

So Ali came. He arrived in Herat at the beginning of November. The next morning, he went to court. He knelt, kissed the Sultan's hand, and offered rich gifts. Masud spoke with him for a long time, about his brother, about money, about the army. Then Ali was asked to wait in a side room. And there, Beyhaqi tells us, about thirty servants seized him, stripped him of his robe and his boots, and put him in heavy chains. His baggage train was plundered the same day.
Masud, it seems, had learned a simple lesson. A man who can give away a throne once can give it away again.

Beyhaqi does not cheer. He says that only God knows what was truly in Ali's heart. And he adds a warning to anyone who trusts this deceitful world, because fortune turns, and the man who stands highest is often the next to fall.

Masud spent that winter in Balkh, the old city in the north of Afghanistan. He arrived in the middle of December. Beyhaqi describes the scene with real joy. The city, he writes, looked like a bride dressed for her wedding. The nobles came with gifts, the court relaxed, and there was music and wine. The struggle was over. The next year, Masud entered Ghazni as Sultan, and the people welcomed him.
But a new reign brings its own accounts to settle. The old supporters of Muhammad were not forgotten. And in Balkh, not long after, one of them would be led out to a gallows. You know his name.
So what does Beyhaqi want us to see in all this?

I think he wants us to see how power really moves. Not always with battles and heroes, but with letters, with silence, with men quietly changing sides on an ordinary autumn day. He shows us a brother who offered peace, and perhaps meant it, and perhaps did not. A general who made kings and forgot that kings remember. And a young man in a fortress, being told that what was meant to be, has been.
Beyhaqi served Masud for many years. He admired him in many ways. But he does not hide the cold side of this victory. That honesty is the whole reason we still read him.
If there is one lesson here, it is this: those who change sides for power should remember that power can change sides too.
Next week, we'll climb up to that fortress. The Brother in the Fortress: what happened to Amir Muhammad, the Sultan who reigned for five months, and how his story ends.

If you enjoyed this story, follow the show so you don't miss the next one, and share it with someone who loves history. I'm Mehdi Rahmani. This episode was retold from the Persian original of the History of Beyhaqi, and narrated with an AI rendering of my own voice. Thank you for listening.

extra_shorts.from: Beyhaqi also gives us a glimpse of Muhammad himself
extra_shorts.hook: Three Persian words that ended a reign
He made a sultan, then unmade him. Then he went to court
